subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is a subtractive process in three-dimensional work?
options: Carving
Modelling in clay
Welding
Casting
questions.explain: Carving removes material from a solid block, making it a subtractive process.

questions.q: In ceramics, what is the technique of building a pot by stacking rolled ropes of clay called?
options: Coiling
Throwing
Slab building
Slip casting
questions.explain: Coiling builds hollow forms by layering and joining rolled coils of clay.

questions.q: Why must clay be fired in a kiln before it can hold water permanently?
options: Firing chemically hardens the clay into a durable ceramic
Firing bleaches the clay a lighter colour
Firing makes the clay softer and easier to shape
Firing adds glaze automatically to the surface
questions.explain: Kiln firing permanently transforms soft clay into hard, durable ceramic material.

questions.q: In three-dimensional design, what is meant by 'negative space'?
options: The empty space around and within a form
The solid mass of the object
The shadow cast by the object
The texture on the object's surface
questions.explain: Negative space is the empty area surrounding or enclosed by the solid form.

questions.q: What is the process of joining two pieces of metal by melting them together called?
options: Welding
Carving
Coiling
Moulding
questions.explain: Welding fuses metal pieces by melting and joining them at high temperature.

questions.q: In ceramics, what is the liquid clay used to join pieces together called?
options: Slip
Glaze
Grog
Flux
questions.explain: Slip is watered-down clay used as an adhesive to join clay pieces.

questions.q: Which material would be most suitable for a lightweight, easily shaped maquette to test a design idea quickly?
options: Card or paper
Cast bronze
Solid marble
Sheet steel
questions.explain: Card and paper are cheap, light and quick to cut and fold for testing ideas.

questions.q: A small preliminary three-dimensional model made to test a design is known as a what?
options: Maquette
Palette
Armature
Kiln
questions.explain: A maquette is a scale model used to develop and test a 3D design.

questions.q: Why is an armature often used when modelling a large clay or plaster figure?
options: It provides an internal framework that supports the weight of the material
It adds colour to the finished surface
It speeds up the drying of the clay
It removes air bubbles from the clay
questions.explain: An armature is an internal skeleton that stops soft material collapsing under its own weight.

questions.q: Casting involves which of the following?
options: Pouring a liquid material into a mould to set into a shape
Cutting away material from a solid block
Bending sheet material into a form
Weaving strips of material together
questions.explain: Casting pours molten or liquid material into a mould where it sets into the desired form.

questions.q: A student wants a sculpture to be viewed and understood from every angle. Which quality should they prioritise?
options: A form resolved 'in the round' so all viewpoints work
A single decorated front face only
A flat relief attached to a wall
Bright surface colour over form
questions.explain: Sculpture 'in the round' is designed to be seen from all sides, so every viewpoint must work.

questions.q: In clay slab building, pieces of flattened clay are joined by scoring and adding slip. What does 'scoring' mean?
options: Scratching cross-hatched marks into the joining surfaces
Smoothing the surfaces flat
Painting the surfaces with glaze
Heating the surfaces with a torch
questions.explain: Scoring roughens the surfaces so the slip can key them together into a strong join.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'relief' sculpture from a freestanding sculpture?
options: A relief projects from a flat background surface
A relief can only be made from metal
A relief is always life-sized
A relief has no texture
questions.explain: Relief sculpture is attached to and raised from a background rather than being fully three-dimensional in the round.

questions.q: A student's clay pot cracks repeatedly while drying. Which is the most likely cause to investigate?
options: Uneven thickness and trapped air causing uneven drying
Using too much water to smooth the surface once
Firing the pot too many times
Using a wheel instead of coiling
questions.explain: Uneven walls and trapped air dry and shrink at different rates, causing stress cracks.

questions.q: Why is wire commonly used in three-dimensional construction work?
options: It can be bent to describe line and structure in space
It cannot hold any shape once bent
It dissolves in water for easy removal
It can only be used flat on a surface
questions.explain: Wire holds a bent shape, letting artists draw linear forms and structures in three dimensions.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a 'found' material used in assemblage?
options: Discarded scrap metal and objects
Freshly mixed plaster
A newly bought block of clay
Liquid resin
questions.explain: Assemblage combines found or discarded objects into a three-dimensional artwork.

questions.q: How does 'scale' affect the way a three-dimensional work is experienced?
options: The size relative to the viewer changes its impact and presence
Scale only matters for two-dimensional drawings
Scale refers only to the colour of the work
Scale has no effect once a work is finished
questions.explain: The physical size of a work in relation to the viewer strongly shapes its presence and effect.

questions.q: A student is designing a tall, thin standing structure that keeps toppling. Which change would most improve its stability?
options: Widen and weight the base
Make the top heavier
Use thinner material throughout
Remove any base entirely
questions.explain: A wider, heavier base lowers the centre of gravity and increases stability.

questions.q: Modelling is best described as which type of three-dimensional process?
options: An additive process, building up a soft material
A subtractive process, cutting away material
A process of melting metals together
A process of pouring liquid into moulds
questions.explain: Modelling adds and shapes pliable material such as clay, making it an additive process.

questions.q: Why might an artist test joining and construction methods on samples before making a final 3D piece?
options: To check which methods are strong and suitable before committing
Because samples are always the finished artwork
To avoid recording any research
Because final pieces never need planning
questions.explain: Testing on samples lets the artist evaluate strength and suitability before making the final work.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Art and Design specifications; Three-Dimensional Studies
